Pregnancy

A baby born at 24 weeks: survival, neonatal care and development

Updated: November 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A baby born at 24 weeks can survive with specialist neonatal care, but no week or percentage predicts one baby's future. Birth this early is a medical emergency and usually means a prolonged neonatal admission. Your maternity and neonatal teams should explain the immediate plan, what is uncertain and how the baby's changing condition affects decisions.

What 24 weeks means

At 24 weeks, a baby is extremely premature. The lungs, skin, feeding skills and nervous system are still developing. Survival is possible, including for some babies born earlier, but it depends on the individual circumstances and available care. It is inaccurate to describe every birth before 24 weeks as hopeless or every birth at 24 weeks as having the same outcome.

Ask the team to use your best pregnancy dates and the exact gestation, such as 24 weeks and 2 days. Growth, birthweight, infection, a singleton or multiple pregnancy, treatment before birth and the place of birth can affect the outlook. These are clinical factors to discuss, not a checklist for predicting the outcome yourself.

Preterm birth is a range

Preterm means birth before 37 completed weeks of pregnancy. WHO groups births before 28 weeks as extremely preterm, from 28 to before 32 weeks as very preterm, and from 32 to before 37 weeks as moderate to late preterm. A baby born at 24 weeks belongs to the first group; the categories do not create a sudden guarantee of safety at a boundary.

Early birth may follow spontaneous labour or may be recommended because continuing pregnancy is more dangerous for the pregnant person or baby. Sometimes no clear cause is found. Antenatal care can identify risks and offer selected preventive treatments, but cannot prevent every premature birth. This is not evidence that a parent failed or that the baby chose to arrive early.

How to read a survival estimate

Always ask which country, hospitals, birth years and babies a number describes, and whether survival means discharge from neonatal care or a later age. In the England and Wales 2020–2021 data reproduced in BAPM's 2026 framework, 483 of 700 liveborn babies at 24 weeks survived to neonatal discharge, about 69%. Among the 669 admitted for neonatal care, the same 483 survivors represented about 72%. These are two denominators, not competing promises.

Figures such as 60% or 68% from older online summaries are not universal chances for a baby born today. Treatment policies, access to intensive care and study populations differ. An online calculator also has a particular dataset and cannot replace the unit's assessment. Ask for the most relevant local information, its uncertainty and what is known about outcomes after discharge, as well as survival.

Preparing if birth may happen soon

If there is time and it is safe, the maternity team may arrange birth in, or transfer to, a centre with the appropriate neonatal intensive care unit. Depending on the situation, treatment before birth can include corticosteroids to help the baby's lungs, magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection, medicines to delay labour briefly, or antibiotics when indicated. These are prescribed decisions, not medicines to start yourself.

More time in pregnancy can help development when remaining pregnant is safe. It is not always safe to delay birth, particularly with infection, bleeding or other serious complications. Do not wait at home to reach another day or finish a treatment course. Ask the obstetric and neonatal teams to explain both the pregnant person's safety and the baby's needs, including what happens if birth progresses quickly.

Fragile skin and keeping warm

A baby this early has very thin, immature skin and limited reserves for keeping warm. Heat and water can be lost easily, so the team monitors temperature, fluids, electrolytes and skin condition. A controlled incubator, and sometimes prescribed humidity or other warming equipment, supports care. Settings are adjusted by trained staff; an ordinary blanket alone is not equivalent to neonatal thermal care.

Handling, adhesives and skin products need particular care. Ask the nurse how to touch and help your baby without disturbing lines or damaging skin; do not apply household creams, oils or extra coverings yourself. Skin-to-skin care is valuable and should be supported as the team judges appropriate, with help and monitoring. Its timing must account for critical illness and respiratory support; it is not a reason to disconnect equipment or postpone necessary stabilisation.

Help with breathing

Immature lungs may lack enough surfactant, the substance that helps the small air spaces remain open. A 24-week baby may need support starting at birth. Depending on their condition, this can include oxygen, continuous positive airway pressure through the nose, or a breathing tube and mechanical ventilation. Surfactant treatment may also be needed; small nasal tubes alone do not describe every baby's treatment.

Staff adjust support using the baby's breathing, oxygen measurements and other tests. More oxygen is not automatically better, and parents should not change settings. Some babies need help for weeks or months and may develop bronchopulmonary dysplasia, a longer-term lung condition. The team should explain the purpose and possible burdens of each treatment and review support as the baby grows or becomes unwell.

Eyes, light and retinal screening

The eyes and visual system are immature, but prematurity alone is not an instruction to keep the eyelids closed with cotton wool or gauze. Neonatal staff manage light exposure and may use incubator covers or specific protection for a procedure or treatment. Eye shields used for jaundice phototherapy have a particular purpose; do not improvise coverings or press on the baby's eyes.

Retinopathy of prematurity, or ROP, affects the developing retinal blood vessels. Mild changes often settle, but severe disease can threaten sight and needs timely specialist treatment. A baby born at 24 weeks needs a planned screening pathway. Ask when examinations start, what was found and when the next check is due. Screening may need to continue after transfer or discharge even if the eyes look normal.

Hearing needs testing too

Hearing is not determined by whether the outer ear looks developed or whether a baby seems to react to a voice. Extremely premature babies have a higher risk of hearing impairment and need the appropriate hearing-screening and follow-up pathway. A response to sound is welcome, but is not a substitute for testing.

The unit should explain the timing and tests for a baby who has needed intensive care. For example, the England NICU pathway uses both automated otoacoustic emissions and an automated auditory brainstem response, which checks responses along the hearing pathway. An unclear screen does not by itself diagnose permanent deafness. Attend any audiology referral, and raise later hearing or communication concerns even after a clear screen.

Brain development and later learning

Some babies born extremely prematurely develop cerebral palsy, difficulties with learning or language, attention or behavioural differences, or visual or hearing impairment. Others have fewer difficulties. Problems may become apparent during infancy or later as developmental demands change. A survival statistic cannot tell you which of these outcomes will apply to your child.

Clinicians use the baby's course, examinations and investigations to update the picture, while recognising uncertainty. Developmental follow-up can identify support needs and connect families with physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy or other services. Disability is not a measure of a child's worth, and neither a reassuring early assessment nor a difficult start settles their entire future.

Feeding and the wider neonatal plan

At 24 weeks, feeding and other organ functions are also immature. Nutrition may initially be given through a vein and later through a tube into the stomach while feeding skills develop. Ask about the individual plan, expressing milk and available feeding support. Needing help or not being able to provide a particular amount of milk is not a reason for blame.

The admission can involve monitoring for infection, bleeding in the brain, intestinal problems and other complications as well as breathing and growth. Not every baby has every complication. Ask what a new test or treatment is for, what results mean now and which changes need a new discussion. Another baby's equipment, length of admission or progress is not a reliable comparison.

Parents belong in the care discussions

Ask for joint, understandable explanations from maternity and neonatal specialists, with an interpreter if needed. Useful questions include what the team expects over the next day, which treatments might help, what their burdens are and how decisions will be reviewed. Your preferences and questions matter, and you should receive support rather than responsibility for making complex decisions alone.

If treatment is unlikely to help the baby, the team may discuss a comfort-focused plan. This remains active care for warmth, relief of discomfort and family contact, not abandonment. Plans may be revisited as more information becomes available. Ask about psychological, practical or bereavement support when needed, and how you can safely participate in daily care.

Discharge and longer-term follow-up

Going home depends on the baby's condition and a safe care plan, not a fixed number of weeks in hospital. Before discharge, get clear instructions for feeds, medicines, any equipment, emergency contacts and planned retinal, hearing and developmental appointments. Ask who coordinates follow-up after a transfer so that a screening visit is not lost between services.

Development is often assessed using corrected age, counted from the original due date, during the first two years. Follow-up schedules vary. NICE's England pathway includes enhanced surveillance for babies born before 30 weeks and a further assessment at four years for those born before 28 weeks. Continue to raise new concerns during childhood; support should respond to the child, not end because an early milestone was reached.

Symptoms and situations that must not wait

Before 37 weeks, contact maternity care immediately for regular contractions or tightenings, period-like pain, unusual backache or leaking fluid; report any bleeding and reduced or changed movements immediately too. After waters have broken, fever, feeling hot/cold/shivery, smelly or greenish fluid, pain or contractions also need immediate advice. For heavy bleeding, or bleeding with severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness, call emergency services. Do not drive yourself.

In hospital, alert the neonatal staff immediately to any worrying change. Outside hospital, get emergency help for a baby with breathing difficulty or very fast breathing, blue/grey/unusually pale or blotchy colour, a non-fading rash, a seizure, unusual sleepiness or difficulty waking, not feeding or responding normally, a weak/high-pitched/continuous cry, or no urine for 12 hours. A temperature of 38°C or more under three months, below 36°C, or feeling cold or shivery also needs emergency assessment. Do not wait for every sign; call an ambulance or have another person drive, and follow your unit's individual emergency plan.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask the maternity and neonatal teams for an individual plan and the exact population, dates and endpoint behind any survival estimate; request an interpreter and written questions if useful.

Ask staff to show safe ways to touch, hold and help your baby. Keep equipment and skin or eye care within the unit's plan rather than copying another baby's treatment.

Before transfer or discharge, confirm the next retinal, hearing and developmental appointments, the coordinator and emergency contacts. Raise symptoms promptly rather than waiting for a scheduled review.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help record the team's explanations, medicines, feeding plan, appointments and your questions. It cannot predict survival, interpret neonatal tests, diagnose a complication or choose respiratory, eye or feeding treatment. Use notes to support conversations; never let tracking delay maternity or emergency care.

When to seek help

Contact maternity care immediately for possible early labour, fluid loss, bleeding or reduced/changed movements; do not postpone a medically needed birth. Emergency pregnancy bleeding signs require emergency services and no self-driving. In hospital, alert neonatal staff to changes immediately. Outside hospital, baby breathing/colour changes, unusual sleepiness or difficulty waking, not feeding/responding normally, a seizure, non-fading rash, abnormal cry or no urine for 12 hours need emergency assessment. So do 38°C or more under three months, below 36°C, or feeling cold/shivery. Do not wait for all signs; call an ambulance or arrange another driver. Follow the unit's emergency and equipment plans.

Evidence notes updated: November 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Survival at 24 weeks is possible, but one percentage cannot predict an individual baby.
  • The population, treatment policy and survival endpoint matter when comparing numbers.
  • Warmth, skin, breathing, feeding and family involvement need a specialist neonatal plan.
  • Retinal and hearing checks, followed by developmental support, remain important after discharge.
  • Do not delay maternity assessment or a medically necessary birth to reach another week.

Frequently asked questions

Do very premature babies develop vision problems?

They have a higher risk, including retinopathy of prematurity, but not every baby develops severe disease. Follow the unit's retinal screening plan, including after discharge. Do not put cotton wool or gauze over the eyes yourself; lighting and any protective equipment are clinical decisions.

Will a baby born at 24 weeks need help breathing?

Breathing support is commonly needed because the lungs are immature. Oxygen, nasal pressure support, ventilation and surfactant are different options selected for the baby. Treatment may change over time; do not assume that all babies need only small nasal tubes.

Can very premature babies have hearing loss?

Yes, the risk is increased, but the appearance of the ears cannot diagnose it. Ask about the intensive-care hearing pathway, attend repeat testing or audiology, and raise later concerns even after a clear newborn screen.

What is preterm birth?

It means birth before 37 completed weeks. Birth before 28 weeks is extremely preterm, so a 24-week birth is in that group. These categories describe gestation; they do not determine one baby's outcome or mean every premature birth could have been prevented.

What is the survival chance at 24 weeks?

There is a real possibility of survival with intensive care, but the answer must be individual. Ask for recent, relevant local data and whether the number counts all live births, treated babies or neonatal admissions. Older online percentages and calculators are not a diagnosis or guarantee.

Should birth always be delayed for another week?

No. Continuing pregnancy helps only when it is safe. Infection, bleeding or other complications can make earlier birth necessary. Contact maternity care immediately for possible early-labour signs and follow the assessment and treatment plan rather than waiting at home.

Does survival mean there will be no later difficulties?

No. Survival, early complications and later development are different outcomes. Some children need support with movement, learning, communication, behaviour, hearing or sight. Follow-up helps identify needs without predicting everything about their future.

When should I seek urgent help?

Possible premature labour, fluid loss, bleeding or changed movements need immediate maternity contact. For a baby outside hospital, breathing or colour changes, difficulty waking, not feeding, a seizure or worrying temperature needs emergency help; do not wait for all signs. Follow the unit's emergency plan and do not drive yourself in an emergency.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
